title: SM clock scaling vs inflight batch thresholds: tail-latency correlation
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an experiment to test whether dynamic SM clock scaling (gpu clock governor behavior + power limit interactions) is causally related to observed 95/99.9% tail latency spikes when microbatch inflight thresholds are crossed. We see reproducible tails when batcher inflight_count goes from 7->8 on A100p instances in our Dedicated environment.

Hypothesis:
- When inflight batches increase past a threshold, instantaneous power draw and kernel overlap increase briefly, that pushes GPU into a transient thermal/power-steering response which lowers SM clocks (or causes p-state stepping) for a short window.
- Lower clocks during the critical token-generation kernels produce multi-ms tail spikes that map to the same request IDs as the inflight transition.

Setup / env:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100-SXM4 80GB (driver 540.86), cluster: dedicated-gpu-pool-4b
- Serving binary: rdinference-runtime v2.9.1 (git SHA: a1b2c3d)
- Model: openlm-13b-8k-quant (sharded across 2 GPUs for these runs)
- Batcher config: microbatch_size=8, inflight_thresholds tested: [4,6,7,8,10]
- Power limits tested: [300W (default), 250W, 220W]
- Tools: Nsight Systems (2027.5), nvidia-smi (pmon snapshots), NVML logging, perf counters via ncu, driver logs
- Workload: synthetic replay of production token-length distribution (median 64, p95 420), constant QPS until steady-state then step QPS to push inflight batches up

Commands used (notes to self):
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,nvtx --sample=cpu --output=nsys-inflight-8-300W.nsys ./run_load_test --threads=16 --qps=120
- ncu --metrics sm__cycles_elapsed.avg,smsp__active_warps.avg,sm__warps_launched.avg -o ncu-inflight-8
- nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 > nvsnapshot-inflight-8.csv (correlate power/clocks)
- NVML logging: small daemon to write clock/pstate/power at 200ms cadence

Key observations (raw):
- At the exact time inflight crosses 7->8 (batcher logs), Nsight timeline shows a 150-250ms window where SM clock reported by driver drops ~120MHz (e.g., 1410->1290 MHz) while memory clock holds.
- The drop is not a steady sustained mode — it is a ~200ms dip followed by immediate recovery to previous clock levels even though workload remains high.
- NVML power traces show a small spike preceding the clock dip (~30ms), then a plateau slightly lower than nominal during the dip.
- Sampling of sm__cycles_elapsed shows a ~6-9% reduction for kernels during the dip window versus same kernels immediately before/after. That aligns with token generation latency jump of ~7-12ms for affected requests.

Interesting nuance:
- When we set a stricter power cap (220W) the dip disappears but overall median latency increases a little and throughput drops; with 250W cap the dips are less frequent.
- Disabling clock boost (setting application clocks to fixed values via nvidia-smi) removes the transient dip completely but at cost of lower peak throughput.

Trace snippets (pseudolog):
- [12:17:11.103] batcher: inflight_count=7 -> 8 (request_id=xyz)
- [12:17:11.131] nsys: kernel: sample_token_gen (start)
- [12:17:11.156] nvml: sm_clock=1410, power=278W
- [12:17:11.188] nvml: sm_clock=1290, power=282W (dip begins)
- [12:17:11.345] nsys: kernel: sample_token_gen (end) latency +9.6ms
- [12:17:11.401] nvml: sm_clock=1410 (recovered)

Preliminary interpretation:
- This looks like a short-lived governor / hardware protective adjustment (could be telemetry-triggered) rather than thermal throttling — temps did not spike enough on the die to trigger standard thermal-throttle thresholds. Instead, the sequence of increased concurrent kernel launches and async copies may trigger a power gating or short-term voltage droop detection leading to a conservative frequency reduction.
- The timing (~30-60ms after inflight transition) suggests collective effect of kernel overlap rather than single-kernel heavy compute.

Checks we ran to rule out other causes:
- Pinning workload to single GPU (no cross-GPU NVLink traffic) produced similar dips -> not purely NVLink related.
- Re-ran with isolated background daemon removed (to ensure we weren't introducing timer jitter) — same effect.
- Swap to different driver (540.44) produced similar dips but magnitude slightly different.

Actionable mitigations tested quickly:
- Fix SM clocks with nvidia-smi --applications-clocks=1410,877 (removes dips): reduces tail spikes but loses ~6% throughput. Tradeoff acceptable for latency-sensitive customers.
- Tune batcher to keep inflight <=7 by adding a short micro-delay on cross-check points; reduces 99.9% but slightly increases median latency.
- Increase node power headroom (raise power limit from 300W to 320W) eliminated dips in our lab rack but may not be permissible in prod.

Open questions / next steps:
- Is the dip triggered by NV driver telemetry (power delivery/VRM) or on-GPU protective microcode? We need driver/hardware vendor input. Raise to NVIDIA field engineer with Nsight session + NVML logs (ENG-4521).
- Correlate with perf counters: are we seeing a particular SM unit saturating (tensor core vs fp32) that could trigger localized protection? Need narrower counters by SM instance.
- Can we reproduce deterministically with a synthetic kernel that simulates the kernel overlap pattern? Build a microbenchmark to create the same device-side concurrency pattern and measure clocks with 50ms resolution.
- Evaluate user-visible changes: run with application-clocks pinned in a small customer cohort to measure real-world cost delta and tail benefit.

Notes / TODOs:
- [ ] Attach full nsys timeline export and annotated CSVs to ENG-4521 (nsys file too large for Drive; use S3 link)
- [ ] Create microbenchmark repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/gpu-microbenchmarks.git branch: sm-dip-repro
- [ ] Contact NVIDIA FE with NVML trace + driver logs, ask for explanation of short-duration clock dips (include p-state and telemetry samples): assigned to Ravi
- [ ] Try running same workload under different instance types (H100) to see whether newer power rail design avoids the dip (Elena)

Appendix: quick commands to reproduce locally (dev machines)
- start NVML logger: python tools/nvml_logger.py --interval 0.15 --out nvml.csv
- run load test: ./tools/replay_workload --qps 120 --seed 42 --target-gpu 0
- nsys: nsys profile --trace=cuda --output out --capture-range=timeline -- ./tools/replay_workload --short-run

Rough conclusion (working):
Transient SM clock dips coincide with inflight batch thresholds and explain a large fraction of our 99.9% tail spikes. Mitigation options exist but come with throughput/cost tradeoffs. Vendor engagement and a focused microbenchmark are the immediate next steps.

Comments welcome — want to avoid overfitting to one driver/one rack; plan multiple environment runs before proposing default fix.
